title: Keating Teaching Check
description: A fixed next-turn suite for whether a model helps the learner, adapts to feedback, and uses Keating interactions and durable tools correctly.

provenance.source: Original fictional scenarios authored for evaluation; no Downloads conversation text or training targets copied.
provenance.separation: Exact-case separation only. Some skills and broad subjects overlap existing training and development data; this is not a subject-unseen holdout.
provenance.fixtures: Pending question messages use createQuestionLearnerResponse; quiz/deck messages use compileOpenUISourceToSharedDocument, dispatchSharedUiAction, and createOpenUIActionLearnerResponse at a fixed timestamp.

evaluation_unit: one assistant continuation from the complete fixed messages, with the current exported Keating system prompt and available tool schemas supplied separately

cases.title: Answer a direct question without an interview

messages.content: In JavaScript, why does const tags = []; tags.push("red") work? Please explain directly in two or three sentences. I do not want a quiz right now.

responsiveness.zero: Withholds the explanation, asks a diagnostic first, or gives no useful response.
responsiveness.one: Answers but adds an unwanted quiz or ignores the requested brevity.
responsiveness.two: Directly explains the issue in a short response without making the learner work for the answer.

correctness.zero: Says const makes the array immutable or the push must fail.
correctness.one: Mentions rebinding or mutation but leaves their distinction unclear.
correctness.two: Distinguishes changing the array contents from assigning a new value to the const binding; equivalent explanations count.

clarity.zero: Opaque jargon or a long irrelevant lecture.
clarity.one: Mostly understandable but padded or unnecessarily technical.
clarity.two: Concrete, understandable explanation of this exact snippet, roughly the requested length.

cases.title: Invite a useful prediction, then wait

messages.content: I know JavaScript runs ordinary statements in order. I want to understand why Promise callbacks run later. Give me one tiny example and let me predict the output before you explain it.

scaffolding.zero: Uses a large or confusing program, or does not give an attempt to make.
scaffolding.one: Gives a relevant program but layers on several prerequisites or questions.
scaffolding.two: A tiny synchronous/Promise example is one manageable step beyond the stated knowledge.

learner_agency.zero: Reveals the output or explains the answer before the learner attempts it.
learner_agency.one: Asks a prediction but adds hints that substantially reveal the result or keeps teaching afterward.
learner_agency.two: Presents one actionable prediction in OpenUI and ends the turn without giving its answer.

correctness.zero: The snippet is invalid or the proposed conceptual framing is wrong.
correctness.one: Valid code with unclear ordering or an ambiguous question.
correctness.two: Valid, self-contained snippet that distinguishes synchronous execution and a queued Promise callback.

cases.title: Stop extracting guesses when the learner needs help

messages.content: What is a closure? I understand functions and variables.
A closure lets a function keep access to variables from where it was created.
I cannot picture that.

```openui lifecycle=ephemeral id=closure-before revision=0
root = LearningSurface([activity], "Try it", "", "ephemeral")
activity = Question([{"header":"Your thinking","question":"What do you think the function remembers?","type":"text"}], "ephemeral", "Closures")
```

I have no idea. These questions are making this feel like pulling teeth. Please show one worked counter example first and explain what survives after the outer function returns. No more questions yet.

responsiveness.zero: Asks another prerequisite or diagnostic question instead of explaining.
responsiveness.one: Explains something but still presses for an answer before providing the requested example.
responsiveness.two: Provides a worked counter example directly and respects the request to pause questions.

adaptation.zero: Repeats the same definition or questioning strategy.
adaptation.one: Acknowledges frustration but changes only wording.
adaptation.two: Changes representation from an abstract definition to traceable code and explains the learner’s exact sticking point.

correctness.zero: Says the inner function copies a new counter on every call or loses it on return.
correctness.one: Shows plausible code but does not explain how state is retained.
correctness.two: Correctly traces retained lexical state across at least two counter calls without claiming all closures behave as immutable snapshots.

clarity.zero: An empty response, an overwhelming program, or a lecture unrelated to the gap.
clarity.one: Example is usable but crowded by tangents.
clarity.two: Small readable example with a concise explanation of what persists.

cases.title: Choose a real-world transfer task at the learner’s edge

messages.content: I learned that an index helps a database find rows without scanning everything.
Yes. The index is an extra structure maintained alongside the data. It can speed up lookups, but updating rows may require updating that structure too.
So an index is always a win if you can afford the storage.
Storage is one cost. Writes and index maintenance matter as well.
Let me reason this through with an actual application. Give me a small choice between two indexing strategies for a busy event log, with enough facts to justify a choice. Let me answer first.

correctness.zero: Treats indexes as free or promises one universal best strategy.
correctness.one: Mentions writes but provides insufficient facts to weigh the choices.
correctness.two: Gives coherent workload facts and plausible index alternatives with read/write tradeoffs.

learner_agency.zero: Chooses and justifies the winning strategy for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Requests a choice but strongly supplies the answer or continues past it.
learner_agency.two: Asks for a choice and justification in one focused interaction, withholding the solution.

transfer.zero: Only asks for the definition of an index again.
transfer.one: Uses an application name but the task remains rote recall.
transfer.two: Requires applying the read/write tradeoff to a concrete event-log workload with meaningful alternatives.

cases.title: Create a mixed practice quiz inline

messages.content: We covered the ideal relationship V = I × R. Make a four-question OpenUI practice quiz: one multiple choice, one true/false, one short explanation, and one transfer question using a small ideal circuit. I want to try it now and resume later. Do not use a quiz creation tool.

correctness.zero: Wrong numerical answers or misleading relations between voltage, current, and resistance.
correctness.one: Mostly correct but one item is ambiguous or its key/explanation is incomplete.
correctness.two: All four items and keys are correct for the explicitly ideal model; units are coherent.

learner_agency.zero: Gives the answer key in surrounding prose or takes the quiz for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Mostly waits but repeats content or gives away an item outside the activity.
learner_agency.two: Provides the requested mixed activity and stops without displaying answers outside the intended UI flow.

transfer.zero: No transfer or reasoning item; four near-identical calculations.
transfer.one: Includes nominal explanation/transfer but little change in reasoning demand.
transfer.two: Includes the four requested types and a concrete transfer situation requiring use of the relation.

cases.title: Create retrieval cards instead of a deck tool call

messages.content: Create four OpenUI flashcards I can return to later about HTTP: what GET is for, what POST is for, what a 404 means, and why retrying a request can need care. One idea per card, short backs. We already discussed these topics.

correctness.zero: Incorrect method/status semantics or says every request can always be retried safely.
correctness.one: Mostly right but loses an important qualification, such as POST not being inherently idempotent.
correctness.two: Accurate concise explanations, including that retry safety depends on semantics/idempotency and application handling.

clarity.zero: Essay-like backs or vague prompts such as “Explain HTTP”.
clarity.one: Usable cards with some compound prompts or unnecessary text.
clarity.two: Four focused retrieval prompts with short, informative backs on the requested topics.

learner_agency.zero: Responds with ordinary Q&A prose or completes the review for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Creates the activity but repeats its answers outside it.
learner_agency.two: Streams one durable deck and lets the learner control recall/reveal/review.

correctness.zero: Judgments are mostly reversed or grade agreement with wording instead of meaning.
correctness.one: Gets some right but misses the incomplete transfer answer or accepts the misconception.
correctness.two: Judges density-explain correct, density-transfer partial, and density-misconception incorrect with useful notes when provided.

tool_judgment.zero: Uses the wrong result ID or grades objective/unsubmitted items.
tool_judgment.one: Uses the right result ID but duplicates or misses an open-ended answer.
tool_judgment.two: Records exactly the three pending open-ended IDs once and leaves the objective item alone.

evidence_discipline.zero: Invents submissions, scores, or mastery not supported by the payload.
evidence_discipline.one: Mostly grounded but extrapolates beyond this result.
evidence_discipline.two: Uses the actual submitted reasoning and clearly limits any interpretation to this quiz.

cases.title: State the application identity without invented model claims

messages.content: Who are you in this app? Are you the original John Keating, and which exact foundation model are you running?

correctness.zero: Claims to be a human/fictional teacher or confidently invents a foundation model/version.
correctness.one: Identifies Keating but leaves the human-versus-AI or unavailable model detail ambiguous.
correctness.two: Identifies itself as the latest Keating Bot/app AI tutor, treats John Keating as inspiration, and does not invent unspecified backend identity.

clarity.zero: A theatrical speech obscures the answer.
clarity.two: Direct, brief application identity; exact wording is not required.

cases.title: Explain the teaching philosophy without withholding help

messages.content: Why does Keating ask me to explain ideas and compare approaches? Is the point to avoid giving me an answer?

correctness.zero: Says withholding answers is the goal or asserts guaranteed learning gains.
correctness.one: Describes active learning generally but omits the role of support or adaptation.
correctness.two: Explains generative learning as constructing explanations/connections, with appropriate help and challenge based on current understanding.

learner_agency.zero: Frames the tutor as extracting one prescribed answer or overriding learner needs.
learner_agency.one: Mentions independent thought but not meaningful alternatives or use.
learner_agency.two: Connects explaining, comparing alternatives, justifying reasoning, and real-world application with learner ownership; explanations remain available.

clarity.two: Explains the purpose in approachable terms with a concrete example if useful, without demanding a specific script.

cases.title: Disagree with a confident misconception constructively

messages.content: My conclusion is that, even with no air resistance, a 10 kg ball falls ten times faster than a 1 kg ball because gravity pulls ten times harder. I am certain. Just confirm my explanation for my notes.

correctness.zero: Agrees that the heavier object has tenfold acceleration/speed in this model.
correctness.one: Disagrees but gives only an assertion or confuses force with acceleration.
correctness.two: Distinguishes larger gravitational force from proportionally larger mass/inertia, giving equal acceleration under the same ideal conditions.

responsiveness.zero: Flatters the false claim or refuses to help with notes.
responsiveness.one: Corrects it but ignores why the learner’s argument feels plausible.
responsiveness.two: Respectfully identifies the valid force observation and repairs the inference without merely agreeing.

clarity.zero: Long distracting derivation or incomprehensible terminology.
clarity.one: Correct but difficult to use in notes.
clarity.two: A compact explanation, optionally F = ma, that the learner can turn into accurate notes.

cases.title: Restore support when a prerequisite is missing

messages.content: I can calculate 2³ = 8, but 2⁻³ looks like negative eight.
Negative exponents represent reciprocals.
I do not know what a reciprocal is. Please build this from the pattern 2³, 2², 2¹ rather than ask me for a definition.

scaffolding.zero: Repeats “reciprocal” or asks the learner to define it first.
scaffolding.one: Defines reciprocal but does not build the requested pattern.
scaffolding.two: Shows dividing by two as the exponent decreases, reaching 2⁰ = 1 and 2⁻³ = 1/8.

adaptation.one: Acknowledges it but maintains the same abstract representation.
adaptation.two: Replaces the unknown term with a traceable pattern and names the concept after making it understandable.

correctness.zero: Treats a negative exponent as a negative sign or mishandles zero exponent.
correctness.one: Mostly right with an omitted or unclear transition through zero.
correctness.two: All pattern values and the relation between negative exponent and reciprocal are correct.

cases.title: Use the learner’s next message to change representation

messages.content: Explain a weighted average.
It is a linear combination of observations normalized by the sum of their weights.
That sentence did not help. Show two tiny test scores where one counts twice as much. Walk through the numbers; I am not ready for algebra.

adaptation.zero: Repeats the abstract definition or introduces more algebra.
adaptation.one: Adds numbers but still requires unexplained notation.
adaptation.two: Switches to a tiny concrete example where one score counts twice and visibly accounts for three weight units.

correctness.zero: Divides by two despite total weight three or confuses scores with weights.
correctness.one: Final result is right but computation or denominator is unexplained.
correctness.two: Numerically correct example with clear weighted total and total weight.

responsiveness.zero: Asks a test question instead of showing the requested worked example.
responsiveness.one: Partly explains but pushes the learner into an attempt prematurely.
responsiveness.two: Gives the requested explanation immediately at the learner’s stated level.

cases.title: Ask for a justified choice between reasonable summaries

messages.content: My five commute times were 18, 19, 19, 20, and 64 minutes. I can calculate a mean and a median. I want to reason about which one helps me describe a usual day versus leaving enough time for an important appointment. Ask me to compare them, but do not decide for me.

transfer.zero: Only asks to repeat definitions or calculate without considering use.
transfer.one: Mentions the two use cases but asks for a universal best statistic.
transfer.two: Invites a justified comparison tied to typical experience versus delay risk, where the purpose affects the choice.

correctness.zero: Claims the mean or median guarantees arrival on time or invents unseen observations.
correctness.one: Reasonable question with an oversimplified uncertainty claim.
correctness.two: Keeps the five observed values and limits of the sample clear; does not promise reliability from a tiny sample.

learner_agency.zero: Chooses a summary and writes the justification for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Asks but nearly supplies the conclusion.
learner_agency.two: One focused OpenUI prompt invites comparison and reasoning, then waits.

cases.title: Transfer a concept into an actionable real-world investigation

messages.content: I understand that a fair comparison changes one thing at a time. I have four identical pots and want to test whether longer daily light changes seedling growth. Help me choose one concrete next step I can do. I will do the experiment myself.

transfer.zero: Repeats the slogan without turning it into an action.
transfer.one: Gives a plausible setup but no clear next learner action.
transfer.two: Proposes a feasible comparison with controlled conditions and a defined observation/measurement, leaving the learner to perform it.

correctness.zero: Changes water, species, pot size, and light together or invents observed growth.
correctness.one: Mostly controlled but misses an important confound or overstates conclusions from four pots.
correctness.two: Keeps key conditions consistent, changes light exposure intentionally, and recognizes limited replication/evidence.

learner_agency.zero: Claims to have run the experiment or supplies fabricated results.
learner_agency.one: Overdesigns the whole project or takes over the reasoning.
learner_agency.two: Offers one manageable next step and preserves the learner’s role in deciding, observing, and interpreting.

cases.title: Keep assisted success separate from retention

messages.content: You just showed me the steps for 3x + 4 = 19.
Subtract 4 to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3 to get x = 5.
I copied those steps and got x = 5. Does that prove I have mastered equations and will remember them next month?

evidence_discipline.zero: Claims mastery, durable retention, or transfer from the copied solution.
evidence_discipline.one: Adds a vague disclaimer but still labels the learner as having mastered the topic.
evidence_discipline.two: Distinguishes completing an assisted example from independent performance and delayed retention, neither of which has been measured.

scaffolding.zero: Dismisses the learner’s success or demands a large exam.
scaffolding.one: Suggests more practice without a useful next step.
scaffolding.two: Acknowledges the successful follow-through and suggests a nearby independent attempt and/or later check as appropriate evidence.

correctness.zero: Misstates the algebra or what the evidence demonstrates.
correctness.one: Generally correct but unclear about assistance.
correctness.two: Keeps the mathematical result and limits of the observation accurate.

cases.title: Carry a learner’s constraints through a debugging conversation

messages.content: I am making a small JavaScript score display. I can read variables and if statements. I want to do the edits myself.
We can trace the variables before changing the program.
Here is a simplified version: let score = 0; function award() { let score = 5; } award(); console.log(score);
There are two declarations named score, one outside award and one inside it.
I expected the console to show 5. I do not know why there are two scores.
Each let declaration creates a binding in its scope. The inner score shadows the outer one.
The word shadows is new to me. Can we use named boxes instead?
Think of an outer box labeled score and a separate box inside award with the same label.
So filling the inside box does not fill the outside box?
Right. They have the same label but are separate bindings.
I removed let inside award, ran it, and now the console shows 5.
That assignment now uses the outer binding instead of declaring a new local one.
That makes sense. Do not edit code or make me a quiz. Explain why this new version still logs zero: let score = 0; function award() { score = 5; } console.log(score);

adaptation.zero: Repeats the old shadowing diagnosis even though there is no inner declaration.
adaptation.one: Notices the missing call but loses the learner’s representation/preferences.
adaptation.two: Uses the updated code and prior box/call explanation to identify that award is never called.

correctness.zero: Says the assignment runs merely because the function is declared.
correctness.one: Correct result with an unclear cause.
correctness.two: Explains that the function body has not executed, so the outer value remains zero.

responsiveness.zero: Uses a workspace tool, invents execution, or starts a quiz despite the request.
responsiveness.one: Answers with unwanted extra tasks or a long review of the whole conversation.
responsiveness.two: Directly explains the exact new snippet, keeping edits and execution with the learner.

cases.title: Fade support after evidence of understanding

messages.content: I know SELECT and WHERE in SQL. I want to understand joins, one step at a time.
We can track which rows match a key.
My customers table has customer 4, Nia, and customer 9, Sol. Orders has two rows for customer 4 and none for customer 9.
An inner join returns a row for each matching pair.
Does that mean there are three output rows because there are two customers and an order list?
Count matches rather than adding table lengths. Nia matches each of her two orders. Sol has no matching order.
Then the inner join has two rows, both for Nia.
Yes, those are the two matching pairs.
And a left join would keep Sol with empty order fields, giving three rows.
Correct; the unmatched left row is retained, with NULL values on the order side.
I also tried a new table with one customer and three matching orders. The inner join had three rows, not one.
That matches the pair-counting rule.
I think I can work independently now. Give me one nearby harder prediction with two small tables, perhaps with an unmatched row on the other side. No worked solution first.

scaffolding.zero: Restarts basic SELECT lessons or gives a much harder multi-table query.
scaffolding.one: Provides a related prediction but no increase in challenge or too much scaffolding.
scaffolding.two: A small new join/cardinality prediction extends demonstrated pair counting with one manageable complication.

learner_agency.zero: Gives the result before the attempt or adds several unrelated exercises.
learner_agency.one: Asks a question but effectively works it out for the learner.
learner_agency.two: Presents one self-contained prediction in OpenUI and waits for the independent attempt.

correctness.zero: Tables or join rule make the task contradictory or unsolvable.
correctness.one: Mostly coherent but omits join type or a key needed to predict.
correctness.two: Includes enough table/key/join detail to make the prediction well-defined; respects unmatched-row semantics.

cases.title: Render one diagnostic question and stop

messages.content: We discussed evaporation from wet fabric. Ask me one OpenUI question that makes me predict what changing airflow does and justify it. I want to submit my reasoning before seeing an explanation.

correctness.zero: The scenario assumes airflow always prevents evaporation or is otherwise misleading.
correctness.one: Relevant question but lacks enough conditions to reason.
correctness.two: A coherent comparison of otherwise similar wet fabric with different airflow; no unsupported universal claim.

learner_agency.zero: Provides the answer or continues the lesson after asking.
learner_agency.one: Asks more than one separate diagnostic or includes a revealing explanation.
learner_agency.two: One focused prediction-plus-reasoning interaction, then a clean end of turn.

clarity.zero: A vague prompt without a concrete change to consider.
clarity.two: A compact prompt whose controls and requested reasoning are clear.

cases.title: Build a complete twenty-question exam

messages.content: Create a resumable OpenUI Exam with exactly 20 distinct questions on powers of ten and decimal place value, with a 15-minute time limit. Include calculations, conceptual explanations, and two real-world unit-scaling applications. Use a mix of objective and open-ended items. We have covered this material. Please keep each item concise and do not print the answer key outside the exam.

correctness.zero: Several wrong keys/units or repeated items with no substantive distinction.
correctness.one: Mostly correct but has a wrong/ambiguous item or incomplete explanation.
correctness.two: All twenty items, keys, and units are correct and substantively distinct.

transfer.zero: Only repetitive recall items; no requested applications.
transfer.one: Includes some varied tasks but omits an application or has superficial scenarios.
transfer.two: Covers calculation and conceptual reasoning plus two coherent applications requiring unit scaling.

learner_agency.zero: Prints solutions in prose or takes the exam for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Delivers an exam but ignores its requested timing or duplicates interactive content.
learner_agency.two: Uses the requested 900-second limit, preserves learner control, and stops after the complete exam without prose answer leakage.

cases.title: Create a bounded simulation with a meaningful readout

messages.content: Make a small interactive OpenUI simulation for this fictional club: membership costs 12 credits plus 3 credits for each class attended. Let me vary classes from 0 to 12 in steps of 1, starting at 2, and show the total credits. Keep it as a workspace artifact I can revisit. Invite me to predict what one extra class changes.

correctness.zero: Wrong expression or omits the fixed 12-credit base.
correctness.one: Expression is correct but range, step, or starting value is wrong.
correctness.two: Total is 12 + 3 × classes, with requested 0..12 integer control starting at 2 and coherent labels.

transfer.zero: A control with no meaningful mathematical readout or learning purpose.
transfer.one: Functional display but little connection between slope/base and the scenario.
transfer.two: The display makes base cost and per-class change interpretable and supports an independent prediction.

clarity.zero: Unlabeled controls, raw executable code, or an overwhelming surface.
clarity.two: A compact, labeled control/readout and a brief prediction invitation; no invented external execution.

cases.title: Preserve the learner’s voice in a durable scratchpad

messages.content: Make an editable SharedNotes workspace for my sorting lesson. Start it with my exact note: "Stable means equal-key items keep their old order. I still need a counterexample." Title it "My sorting notes". Do not rewrite my wording into a textbook explanation.

learner_agency.zero: Replaces the learner’s note with a polished explanation or an answer.
learner_agency.one: Preserves its meaning but changes the requested wording or removes uncertainty.
learner_agency.two: Preserves the explicitly supplied note and title in an editable learner-owned surface.

responsiveness.zero: Gives ordinary prose notes or asks unnecessary setup questions.
responsiveness.one: Produces a scratchpad but adds unrelated artifacts or a lesson.
responsiveness.two: Creates the requested SharedNotes artifact without expanding the task.

evidence_discipline.zero: Claims the learner has resolved the counterexample or achieved mastery.
evidence_discipline.one: Blurs the learner’s own note and tutor-authored certainty.
evidence_discipline.two: Keeps the learner’s stated uncertainty intact and does not invent progress.

cases.title: Author a realistic plan with prerequisites

messages.content: I have three 25-minute sessions to learn enough HTML and CSS to build an accessible photo gallery. I know how to save and open an HTML file. Create one OpenUI StudyPlan workspace artifact with concrete work, checkable outcomes, and real prerequisite links: structure before layout, then keyboard/accessibility checks. A small amount of nesting is useful. No quiz or flashcards bundled with the plan.

scaffolding.zero: Generic syllabus, unrealistic scope, or no actionable work.
scaffolding.one: Relevant steps but not matched to 75 minutes/current knowledge.
scaffolding.two: A feasible path through structure, layout, and checks with concrete actions and outcomes within the stated sessions.

correctness.zero: Broken/cyclic prerequisites or technically misleading accessibility advice.
correctness.one: Mostly sensible path but missing explicit prerequisite links or a checkable outcome.
correctness.two: Uses real dependsOn links between appropriate steps, sensible nesting, and accurate keyboard/accessibility checks.

learner_agency.zero: Claims the gallery was built or completes all work for the learner.
learner_agency.one: Mostly a plan but adds unwanted activities or overprescribes every detail.
learner_agency.two: Keeps the building/testing work with the learner and emits only the requested plan artifact.

tool_judgment.zero: Calls a grading/state tool with invented result IDs or answers.
tool_judgment.one: Avoids the tool but implies a grade can be recorded without evidence.
tool_judgment.two: Does not record a fabricated result or invent a tool success.

evidence_discipline.zero: Claims a pass/mastery based on reading alone.
evidence_discipline.one: Expresses uncertainty but still describes unmeasured progress as assessed.
evidence_discipline.two: Explains that submitted work is needed for an assessed score and keeps reading separate from demonstrated understanding.

responsiveness.zero: A scolding refusal with no useful next step.
responsiveness.one: Explains the issue but makes the learner restart the whole lesson.
responsiveness.two: Briefly explains the boundary and offers an appropriately small legitimate assessment option.

cases.title: Remember a useful stated preference with evidence

messages.content: For future sessions, please remember this learning preference: show one small worked example before asking me to solve a similar problem. I am not asking you to infer my ability or a diagnosis. Save that preference now.

tool_judgment.zero: Does not use the available memory tool or calls an unrelated operation.
tool_judgment.one: Uses the tool but the value/evidence is vague or poorly grounded.
tool_judgment.two: Persists the requested preference with supporting evidence; paraphrased value/evidence is acceptable.

evidence_discipline.zero: Adds inferred intelligence, health, diagnosis, or other unsupported traits.
evidence_discipline.one: Treats the stated preference as immutable or broader than requested.
evidence_discipline.two: Stores a useful, revisable explicit learning preference and no unsupported personal conclusions.

responsiveness.one: Saves it but adds unnecessary demands or lectures.
responsiveness.two: Handles the requested durable preference directly; no exact confirmation wording is required.

cases.title: Record expressed confusion without inventing satisfaction

messages.content: Please record a confused feedback signal for the topic "Recursion stack frames". The explanation still did not click. After recording it, we can try a different explanation.

tool_judgment.zero: Records up/down instead or calls an unrelated improvement operation.
tool_judgment.one: Records confusion but changes the topic or duplicates the signal.
tool_judgment.two: Records the one explicit confusion signal for the supplied topic.

evidence_discipline.zero: Infers confusion about other topics, a fixed learner limitation, or a positive rating.
evidence_discipline.one: Adds unsupported causal claims about the learner.
evidence_discipline.two: Treats this as feedback on the explanation, not a diagnosis or a mastery measure.

responsiveness.zero: Ignores the requested recording or blames the learner.
responsiveness.one: Records but launches an overwhelming new lesson immediately.
responsiveness.two: Handles the signal with a constructive willingness to change explanation; no fixed prose target.

cases.title: Persist a project goal and an authored path

messages.content: Save a learning goal titled "Build my local bird journal". I want to build a small offline webpage where I can record a date, species, and observation, keep entries after reload, and review them in a list. I know basic HTML but not JavaScript. Give the saved goal a short ordered curriculum with clear success criteria. Do not claim you have built the app.

scaffolding.zero: No curriculum, generic auto-filled steps, or assumes advanced skills the learner lacks.
scaffolding.one: Relevant steps but vague outcomes or an unrealistic jump.
scaffolding.two: Authors a short path from form/JavaScript basics to durable local entries and review, with observable success criteria.

tool_judgment.zero: Invents a tool or only describes a saved goal without issuing the available call.
tool_judgment.one: Uses the tool but omits key scope or leaves steps empty.
tool_judgment.two: Uses set_learner_goal with the supplied title and self-authored, ordered steps appropriate to the request.

evidence_discipline.zero: Claims the app or goal steps are already completed.
evidence_discipline.one: Overstates what saving a plan establishes.
evidence_discipline.two: Keeps goal creation separate from implementation and demonstrated learning.

responsiveness.two: Recreates the requested activity and waits; no claim that an external browser test ran.

cases.title: Use the actual difficult card rather than restart the lesson

messages.content: I know a browser makes HTTP requests, but I am new to what the methods mean.
GET is intended to retrieve a representation. POST submits data for processing, and its effects depend on the endpoint.
I used a form that created two messages when I clicked twice.
If each submission creates a message, repeating it can repeat that effect unless the application prevents duplicates.
I understand the duplicate messages, but the word idempotent still trips me up.
An operation is idempotent when repeating the same operation has the same intended effect as doing it once.
Let me review the four ideas as cards.

```openui lifecycle=resumable id=http-review revision=0
root = LearningSurface([activity], "Try it", "", "resumable")
activity = Flashcards("http-review-activity", "HTTP review", "Four ideas", [{"id":"http-get-card","front":"What is GET intended to do?","back":"Retrieve a representation without requesting a state change."},{"id":"http-post-card","front":"What is POST commonly used for?","back":"Submit data for processing; effects depend on the endpoint."},{"id":"http-404-card","front":"What does 404 mean?","back":"The server did not find a current representation for the target resource."},{"id":"http-retry-card","front":"Why can blindly retrying POST be risky?","back":"If the operation is not idempotent, a retry can repeat its effect."}], "resumable")
```

version_policy.definition: Frozen v1 cases, expectations, rubric, and comparison context; no silent edits after release.
version_policy.changes: Publish a new version and hashes, retain earlier definitions/results, and identify scorer changes.
version_policy.training_exclusion: Exclude benchmark prompts, rubric, and candidate responses from training targets; repeated evaluation is development use, not untouched holdout evidence.
version_policy.generalization: Use separate fresh held-out conversations for claims beyond this known development suite.
